~5,000 users expected in the first year, EU-based
Real-time notifications planned for a later phase
ambiguities: Assumed relational data model (projects, tasks, users) — confirm if document-style storage is acceptable
Assumed standard latency tolerance; no real-time requirement in v1

options.name: Serverless-First
options.summary: Fully managed, pay-per-request stack. Zero servers to patch, scales automatically, cheapest at low traffic.

services.name: Amazon CloudFront
services.role: CDN for frontend assets and API edge caching

services.name: Amazon API Gateway
services.role: REST API entry point, rate limiting, request validation

services.name: AWS Lambda
services.role: Stateless business logic, scales to zero

services.name: Amazon EventBridge
services.role: Event bus for future async workflows (notifications)

options.rationale: At 5,000 users the request volume is low enough that pay-per-request pricing keeps the bill minimal. No infrastructure to operate means a solo founder can ship and sleep.

pros: Lowest cost at this traffic level
Automatic scaling with no capacity planning
cons: DynamoDB data model requires upfront design discipline; joins are painful
Vendor lock-in is deepest with this option
Debugging distributed Lambda flows is harder
tradeoffs.best_when: You want minimal ops burden, your data model is access-pattern-driven, and you value speed over flexibility.

assumptions: DynamoDB on-demand mode, no provisioned capacity

options.scalability_ceiling: Effectively unlimited; DynamoDB and Lambda scale horizontally by design
options.security_posture: Strong managed defaults; IAM-scoped Lambda roles, no exposed servers

options.name: Container on Fargate
options.summary: Dockerized app on ECS Fargate with managed PostgreSQL. Classic SaaS shape with no servers to patch.

services.name: Amazon CloudFront
services.role: CDN in front of the app and API

services.name: Application Load Balancer
services.role: Routes traffic to containers, TLS termination

services.name: Amazon ECS Fargate
services.role: Runs API and web containers without managing EC2

options.rationale: A relational project/task/user model maps naturally to PostgreSQL. Fargate removes server management while keeping a familiar request/response architecture that any developer can debug.

pros: PostgreSQL fits relational SaaS data perfectly
Familiar stack — easy to hire for
Containers are portable if you ever leave AWS
cons: Higher baseline cost than serverless at low traffic
You still manage container orchestration config
Scaling requires autoscaling policies, not magic
tradeoffs.best_when: Your data is relational, you want predictable latency, and you plan to grow the team.

options.scalability_ceiling: ~50,000 concurrent users before database sharding is needed
options.security_posture: Strong; private subnets, WAF, encryption at rest via KMS, IAM-scoped tasks

options.name: Classic EC2 + RDS
options.summary: EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group behind an ALB with RDS PostgreSQL. Maximum control, most ops work.
options.rationale: The most battle-tested shape on AWS. Every knob is adjustable, every problem is documented online. Chosen when you need full control of the OS layer.

pros: Full control over OS, runtime, and networking
Cheapest compute at sustained high utilization (with savings plans)
cons: You patch OS, manage AMIs, and handle SSH access
Highest operational burden for a solo developer
tradeoffs.best_when: You have specific OS-level requirements or sustained heavy compute that makes reserved capacity cheaper.

options.scalability_ceiling: Similar to container option; bounded by database, not compute
options.security_posture: Good if hardened manually; security groups, IAM roles, and patching are your responsibility

recommendation.rationale: Your data model (projects, tasks, users, permissions) is relational, which makes PostgreSQL the natural fit — and that rules out the serverless option's DynamoDB-centric design for a team without NoSQL modeling experience. Between containers and EC2, Fargate removes the entire OS-patching burden, which matters enormously for a solo developer or tiny team. The ~$180/month premium over serverless buys you predictable latency, a portable architecture, and a stack any future hire already knows. At 5,000 users you're comfortably inside the budget ceiling, and GDPR is satisfied by pinning everything to eu-central-1 with KMS encryption.

why_not_others.reason: Cheapest, but DynamoDB would force you to re-model relational project/task data around access patterns — a common source of painful rewrites at month 6. Cold starts also hurt perceived quality for a productivity tool.
Maximum control you don't need at 5,000 users, in exchange for OS patching and AMI management that will eat a solo founder's weekends. Slower scaling is a liability if you go viral.
